summary.text: Descriptive statistics are numbers or simple graphs that summarize features of a sample of data.
Common summaries are measures of central tendency such as the mean, median and mode, and measures of variability such as the standard deviation.
Unlike inferential statistics, they aim to summarize the sample itself rather than learn about the wider population it represents.

items.prompt: A basketball player has a shooting percentage of 33%. About how many shots go in?
items.explain: A player who shoots 33% is making approximately one shot in every three.

items.prompt: Why is a grade point average a descriptive statistic?

options.label: It predicts how a student will score next
It is found by sampling a whole population
It ranks two different students against each other
One number sums up performance across many courses

items.explain: The grade point average is a single number that describes the general performance of a student across the range of their course experiences.

items.prompt: A researcher wants to describe how spread out some measurements are, not their typical value. Which measure fits?
items.explain: The standard deviation is a measure of variability, while mean, median and mode measure central tendency.

items.prompt: A medical report only tabulates the sample size in each treatment group and draws no conclusion beyond them. What is it doing?
items.explain: Descriptive statistics aim to summarize a sample rather than use the data to learn about the wider population.

items.prompt: Someone wants to describe how two different variables, such as height and weight, move together. Which kind of measure fits?
items.explain: Bivariate analysis describes the relationship between two variables, with quantitative measures of dependence such as correlation and covariance.

items.prompt: A study draws its main conclusions with inferential statistics. Why does its first table still list sample sizes and group characteristics?

options.label: Descriptive statistics are generally presented as well
The table is required to reject a null hypothesis
Inferential statistics cannot be reported without it
The table replaces the main conclusions

items.explain: Even when the main conclusions come from inferential statistics, descriptive statistics are generally also presented.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: A study draws its main conclusions with inferential statistics.
Its first table lists the overall sample size and subgroup sizes.
That table is a set of descriptive statistics.
So descriptive statistics never appear alongside inferential ones.

beats.idea: Descriptive statistics squeeze a sample into a few summary numbers or graphs that show its typical value and its spread.

paragraphs.heading: Summing up data
paragraphs.text: A descriptive statistic is a number that sums up some feature of a collection of information. Descriptive statistics, as an activity, is the work of using and analysing such numbers. The summaries can be quantitative, called summary statistics, or visual, in the form of simple graphs that are easy to understand.

paragraphs.heading: Describing, not inferring
paragraphs.text: The goal is to summarize the sample in hand, not to learn about the larger population it may stand for. That aim separates it from inferential statistics, and it generally means descriptive statistics is not built on probability theory. Even studies whose main conclusions are inferential usually present descriptive statistics as well. A paper on human subjects, for example, typically has a table of sample sizes, overall and for key subgroups, plus traits such as average age and the share of each sex.

paragraphs.heading: Center and spread
paragraphs.text: Commonly used summaries include measures of central tendency and measures of variability, also called dispersion. Central tendency is described by the mean, median and mode. Variability is described by the standard deviation or variance, the range and quartiles, and the minimum and maximum values. Indices such as skewness and kurtosis describe the overall shape of the distribution.

paragraphs.heading: Everyday examples
paragraphs.text: Sport and school offer familiar cases. In basketball, a shooting percentage is shots made divided by shots taken, so a player shooting 33% makes about one shot in every three. That single number sums up many separate events. A grade point average does the same for a student, describing general performance across all of their courses.

paragraphs.heading: One variable or two
paragraphs.text: Describing a single variable is called univariate analysis, and its distribution can be shown in tables or in graphs such as histograms and stem-and-leaf displays. Bivariate analysis goes further and describes the relationship between two variables. Measures of that link include correlation, for instance Pearson's r for two continuous variables, or Spearman's rho when at least one is not continuous, and covariance, which reflects the scale the variables are measured on.

paragraphs.heading: Old roots, newer tools
paragraphs.text: Summarizing data is old: the simple tabulation of populations and economic data was the first form statistics took. More recently, a set of summary techniques has been gathered under the name exploratory data analysis, and the box plot is one of them. A practical trick for highly skewed data is to take logarithms, which makes graphs more symmetrical and closer to the normal distribution, so they are easier to grasp intuitively.
